text: You tell someone you want to make more money, and suddenly the advice starts: “Don’t get too obsessed.”
“Money isn’t everything.”
“Be grateful for what you have.”
But why does wanting more money sound, to some people, like wanting to become a worse person?
Part of the answer begins with the stories we hear growing up.
The wealthy villain cares only about profit, while the humble hero has very little but always does the right thing.
At home, we might hear, “Rich people are greedy,” or, “Money changes people.”
Sometimes, those beliefs come from painful experiences.
A parent worked for someone who underpaid them.
A family watched a dishonest person get rich while honest people struggled.
Those experiences deserve to be taken seriously.
But a belief about someone’s behavior can become a belief about wealth itself.
“Some people make money by hurting others” becomes “Making money means hurting others.”
Once those ideas get connected, even ordinary financial goals can feel morally suspicious.
You want enough savings to handle an emergency.
You want to help your parents, afford a comfortable home, or leave a job that makes you miserable.
Yet you still wonder whether wanting more makes you selfish.
Money also raises questions about fairness.
When someone becomes wealthy, people want to know how it happened.
Did they build something useful?
Inherit an advantage?
Take a risk?
Or benefit at someone else’s expense?
These are reasonable questions, especially when people have seen businesses mistreat workers or sell promises they cannot keep.
The trouble comes when we assume the answer before we know the circumstances.
Someone says, “I want to earn more,” and we hear, “I’ll do anything to get rich.”
But earning more could mean learning a useful skill, negotiating better pay, or building an honest business.
The ambition alone doesn’t tell us how someone intends to act.
There is also a more personal reason money makes people uncomfortable: belonging.
If you grew up around financial struggle, shared difficulties may be part of how your family connects.
Everyone understands the same worries and makes similar sacrifices.
When your circumstances improve, you might fear becoming distant from them.
Will your friends think you’re showing off?
Will your family assume you feel superior?
Will people still recognize you?
Sometimes, guilt about making money includes a fear of losing connection.
And sometimes, criticism from others carries that same fear.
“Don’t forget where you came from” can mean, “When your life changes, will there still be room for us?”
Then comes the difficult question: when does wanting more become wanting too much?
Wanting to cover rent seems understandable.
Building an emergency fund sounds responsible.
But what about wanting a bigger house, an earlier retirement, or a successful business?
People draw the line in different places because money means different things to them.
For one person, it means safety.
For another, freedom.
For someone else, recognition—the chance to prove they finally matter.
Those motives can overlap.
You might want to provide for your family and impress people who doubted you.
That makes it useful to ask what you expect the money to accomplish.
Will it solve a practical problem?
Give you control over your time?
Or are you hoping a particular income will finally make you feel worthy?
Examining your motivation can help you decide whether the goal will give you what you need.
And yes, the pursuit of money can become harmful.
It can happen when someone excuses dishonesty because a deal is profitable, repeatedly sacrifices relationships, or treats other people as valuable only when they help generate income.
Those are meaningful concerns.
But an income figure cannot tell you someone’s character.
You have to look at their choices: How are they earning it?
Who benefits?
Who bears the cost?
Are they being honest about what they offer?
If you feel guilty about wanting more money, finish this sentence: “I want more money because…”
Be specific.
Maybe you’re tired of being one unexpected bill away from panic.
Maybe you want to spend more time with your children.
Maybe you want to build something you care about.
Then decide which boundaries you’ll keep while pursuing that goal.
What promises won’t you make?
What work won’t you accept?
What relationships and responsibilities will you protect?
You can appreciate what you have while wanting your circumstances to improve.
You can care about inequality while asking to be paid fairly.
You can pursue success and remain accountable for your actions.
So why do people think making more money is evil?
Sometimes, they have witnessed real harm.
Sometimes, they are repeating beliefs they inherited.
Sometimes, they fear greed, change, or losing people they love.
Understanding those concerns helps us judge financial ambition more thoughtfully.
Because saying you want more money still leaves the most revealing question unanswered: what are you willing to do for it?
